title: Part-to-Whole Without Pie Lies
objective: After this lesson you will be able to show shares with stacked bars/treemaps, restrict pies to 2–4 familiar shares, and normalize shares that don't sum (overlaps, missing other) explicitly.
why: Pies dominate dashboards and disappoint readers: 12 slices defeat angle judgment, similar shares blur, and missing 'other' inflates shares silently. Part-to-whole has better shapes (100% stacked bars sortable, treemaps for hierarchies) with pies reserved for the rare case they serve (few familiar shares, one emphasized part). Share honesty is normalization honesty.

blocks.text: Pies work for **2–4 familiar shares** (market halves, budget split) and **one emphasized part vs rest** (our share vs market). Beyond that, angles fail: 12-slice pies rank nothing, similar slices merge visually, legends force color-matching labor. The test: can readers rank all parts in 5 seconds? No → bars.

blocks.caption: Normalization with a 100-check: shares that don't sum lie by construction

blocks.text: **100% stacked bars** compare compositions across groups (mix by quarter, sortable, shared baseline). **Treemaps** show hierarchical shares (category → subcategory areas, labeled). **Waffle/unit charts** make small shares countable (each square = 1%). All beat pies on rankability while keeping part-to-whole readable.

blocks.title: Percentages need populations
blocks.text: Every share states its whole (share of what, among whom, over what window) — shares without populations compare nothings. '60% prefer X' means nothing until the denominator is named.

blocks.title: Normalize the shares
blocks.note: Run it: shoes≈57.8%, hats≈33%, apparel≈9.3%, summing to ~100 (rounding dust noted, not hidden). Shares normalized explicitly with the sum check — then pick bars over pie for three ranked parts.

items: Pies for 2–4 familiar shares or one-vs-rest only; rankability test decides the rest
Stacked bars (sortable compositions), treemaps (hierarchies), waffles (countable small shares)
Normalize explicitly with sum-checks; overlaps need stated basis, never silent sums

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice normalizer and confirm shares + sum check. (b) Argue bars vs pie for these three parts with the rankability test. (c) State how overlapping categories (item in two groups) must be handled before any share math.
hints: Rank test: order the three shares in 5 seconds from pie angles vs bar lengths — bars win by construction.
Overlaps: split attribution or state basis (share of revenue with multi-count noted); silent sums double-count.
exercise.why: Normalization proof (sum checks), rankability argument (encoding precision), and overlap discipline (basis stated) are the three composition judgments.
exercise.code: // Share pattern: normalize + sum-check + rankability test + overlap basis.

quiz.q: 12-slice market pie in a deck. Fix?
options: Sorted bars (or treemap for hierarchy): 12 angles rank nothing; position encodes precisely
quiz.explain: Rankability test fails at 12 slices: angles blur, legends labor. Bars rank; treemaps hierarchize.

quiz.q: Shares sum to 140% silently. Cause + fix?
options: Overlapping categories double-counted: split attribution or state basis (share of X with multi-count noted)
quiz.explain: Sums over 100 expose overlap: items counted multiply. Basis stated explicitly or attributions split — silent sums lie by construction.

options: 2–4 familiar shares or one-vs-rest emphasis where angles suffice and rankability isn't needed
quiz.explain: Narrow license: few familiar parts or single emphasis. Beyond that, precision channels (bars) take over.

summary: Rankable compositions via bars/treemaps, pies on narrow license, normalized shares with sum checks, overlaps with stated basis. Parts honest to wholes.
next: Shares settled — now variables against each other: scatters, confounders, and causation discipline. Next: relationships without illusions.
